A [[power forward]], his [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) career spanned from 1983 to 1999 with the [[Utah Jazz]] and the [[Minnesota Timberwolves]]. Bailey has been a [[broadcast analyst]] for the Utah Jazz and the [[University of Utah]]— in addition to work as an [[inspirational speaker]], singer, songwriter, and film actor. Bailey garnered the nickname "Big T" during his basketball career. == Playing career == Bailey attended [[North Carolina State University]] and was a leader in the Wolfpack's miracle run to the [[1983 NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Tournament|1983 NCAA Championship]]. That year, under head coach [[Jim Valvano]], he led the Wolfpack in both scoring and rebounding. The [[Utah Jazz]] selected him as the 7th pick of the [[1983 NBA draft]]. Jazz management reported that he was selected for the quality of his character, as well as the quality of his game. This was the beginning of 16 years of playing professional basketball, with 12 of those years in the NBA. Bailey's career-high points game came on March 14, 1988, when he scored 41 points and grabbed 8 rebounds in a 116–115 win over the [[Denver Nuggets]].{{cite web |title=Thurl Bailey Career High 41 Versus Nuggets |url= https://www.statmuse.com/nba/ask/thurl-bailey-career-high-points |website=Statmuse |access-date=24 February 2022}} Bailey was a starter with the Jazz for most of his first two seasons, but with the drafting of [[Karl Malone]], Jazz coach [[Frank Layden]] made Bailey one of the first options off the bench. As a result, Bailey had his two finest NBA seasons in 1987–88 (19.6 ppg, played in all 82 games and started ten times) and 1988–89 (19.5 ppg, 82 games, three starts). Both seasons saw him finish second in the [[NBA Sixth Man of the Year Award|Sixth Man of the Year]] voting. During Bailey's Utah tenure, he played in 665 games, missing only four games in which he was eligible to play.{{cite web |title=IT'S T FOR TY AS JAZZ DEAL THURL TO MINNESOTA |url= https://www.deseret.com/1991/11/26/18953813/it-s-t-for-ty-as-jazz-deal-thurl-to-minnesota |website=Deseret News |access-date=24 February 2022}} On November 25, 1991, he was traded by the Jazz along with a 1992 second-round draft pick to the Minnesota Timberwolves for [[Tyrone Corbin]]. Bailey holds the unusual distinction of playing 84 combined regular-season games during the 1991–92 season for both teams. He played for almost three seasons in Minnesota, until 1994, when he left the NBA and played in the [[A1 Ethniki|Greek League]] (playing for [[Panionios Forthnet|Panionios]]) for the 1994–95 season.[http://www.nba.com/playerfile/thurl_bailey/bio.html Thurl Bailey NBA.com bio] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090419140135/http://www.nba.com/playerfile/thurl_bailey/bio.html |date=2009-04-19 }} From 1995 to 1998, he played in the [[Serie A (basketball)|Italian League]] for [[Pallacanestro Cantù|Polti Cantù]] in 1995–97 and [[Olimpia Milano|Stefanel Milano]] in 1997–98, before returning to the Jazz as a [[free agent]] on January 21, 1999. He retired after the end of the 1998–99 season. ==Post-playing career== Bailey is a [[public speaker]], a broadcast analyst for the Utah Jazz and the [[University of Utah]], an actor, and a singer/songwriter.{{cite web | url=http://vault.sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1030363/index.htm | title=Thurl Bailey, Forward | publisher=SI Vault | author=Luis Fernando Llosa | date=2003-11-03 | access-date=2009-06-01 | archive-date=2012-07-17 | archive-url=https://archive.today/20120717005558/http://vault.sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1030363/index.htm | url-status=dead }} Bailey's albums include ''Faith in Your Heart'' (1998), ''The Gift of Christmas'' (2001), and ''I'm Not the Same'' (2002). Bailey is chairman of Big T Productions, Fertile Earth (which has a [[patent]] pending on a fertilizer that works through [[irrigation sprinkler]] systems), and FourLeaf Films. He works with various charities, including [[Make-A-Wish]], [[Drug Abuse Resistance Education|D.A.R.E.]], and the Happy Factory. Bailey continues to coach in the Salt Lake City area using the private coaching service [[CoachUp]].[http://www.coachup.com/coaches/thurlb www.coachup.com/coaches/thurlb] ==Personal life== Bailey was born in Washington, D.C., and grew up in a high-crime neighborhood of [[Seat Pleasant, Maryland]] bordering D.C. He was a graduate of [[Bladensburg High School]] in [[Bladensburg, Maryland]]{{cite news|url=http://www.deseretnews.com/article/460030429/Thurl-Baileys-wonderful-life.html?pg=all|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131021192612/http://www.deseretnews.com/article/460030429/Thurl-Baileys-wonderful-life.html?pg=all|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 21, 2013|title=Thurl Bailey's wonderful life|last=Robinson|first=Doug|date=22 February 2003|work=[[Deseret News]]|access-date=18 August 2016}} Bailey is the father of six children. He has a daughter, Chonell, with his high school sweetheart and two sons, Thurl Jr., and TeVaun from his first marriage. Bailey and his wife, Sindi ([[née]] Southwick), live in [[Highland, Utah]] with their three children BreElle, Brendan, and Bryson. His son Brendan played basketball at Marquette. Bailey was raised [[Baptist]].{{cite news|title=Former NBA Star Thurl Bailey Shares Incredible Conversion Story|url=http://www.ldsliving.com/Former-NBA-Star-Thurl-Bailey-Shares-Incredible-Conversion-Story/s/82134|access-date=20 August 2016|work=[[LDS Living]]|date=17 May 2016}} While playing basketball in Italy, Bailey decided to join [[the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]]. He was baptized on December 31, 1995.{{cite web | url=http://www.playingfieldpromotions.com/Thurl-Bailey.php | title=Thurl Bailey Biography | author=Playing Field Promotions | access-date=18 August
